title: Lesson 40: Stateful vs Stateless Agents: Context, Memory, and Tool State
description: Why a language model remembers almost nothing and knows a great deal, and how context, memory, and tool state become the architecture that decides whether an agent is useful on day thirty.

questions.question: What is the difference between context and memory in an agent?
options: Context survives beyond the window; memory is what is in the window now.
Context is what is in the window now; memory survives beyond it.
Context lives in the database; memory lives in the model's fixed weights.
They are the same thing, measured in different units of time.
questions.explanation: Context is the set of tokens in the window right now, while memory is the selective state retained across interactions and stored outside the model.

questions.question: Which task is best served by a stateless design?
options: A long-running support workflow that spans many days.
A coding assistant that must recall earlier design decisions.
One-shot classification where each request is independent.
An agent that resumes a complex claim across separate sessions.
questions.explanation: Extraction, classification, and one-shot calls are independent requests with no continuity to keep, so statelessness keeps them simple and easy to scale.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a memory layer to the question it answers?
options: Semantic memory answers what happened; episodic memory answers what is true.
Procedural memory stores domain facts; semantic memory stores routines.
Working memory stores durable facts; long-term memory holds the window.
Semantic memory is what is true; episodic memory is what happened.
questions.explanation: Semantic memory holds durable facts about what is true, while episodic memory records time-indexed experiences and answers what happened.
